text:
One of the biggest objections we get from banks is "It's too smart. We can't afford to let it help our customers this much."
 
The first time I heard that, I almost teared up in the room. I'm a 31 year old man and I've spent my whole career trying to build products that help people. Now that I finally had one, the people I was selling it to were telling me they didn't want it to help.
 
It made me question the industry I was serving. For a while it made me question the incentives of the entire banking system.
 
Then I actually dug into what they were saying.
 
It wasn't greed. It was the business model.
 
A bank makes most of its money on the spread. It pays you a little on the money you leave with it and earns a lot lending that money out. That gap is widest when you aren't paying attention. Cash sitting in checking at 0.01%. An overdraft fee you didn't see coming. A CD that rolled over at whatever rate was on the screen that day.
 
None of that is a scam. It's just that a real chunk of a bank's earnings depends on customers not optimizing.
 
So when I show up with an agent that looks at your accounts and says "you have $40,000 sitting idle, move it and earn $1,600 a year," I'm not offering that bank a feature. I'm offering to shrink its margin one customer at a time.
 
That's when it stopped feeling personal.
 
But the customer is getting that agent either way. From us, from the bank, or from something on their phone that reads their statements. The information edge the banker used to have is gone. The customer's agent knows every rate and every fee, and it works for them, even when the banker's incentives don't.
 
The innovative banks already see this. They've stopped trying to earn on inattention and started trying to earn on trust. Be the place where the customer's money actually lives and get paid on the relationship, the lending, and the payments that come with it. That model gets stronger as the customer gets smarter. The old one gets weaker.
 
Which has changed how I think about partners.
 
The banks that care deeply about their customers want the agent as smart as it can be. Those turn out to be the ones we do our best work with.
 
The ones that want their customers only as smart as they allow aren't bad people. They're defending a model their customers are about to outgrow.
 
The last era of banking was built on what the customer didn't know.
 
The next one gets built by the banks that make their customers smarter and give them a reason to stay.
 
A customer who stays because they never looked is an account. A customer who looks at everything and stays anyway is a relationship.

We just launched gold and silver perpetuals in the US.

And commodity derivatives are now our fastest-growing product.

Markets started with grain and metals, expanded into rates, indices, and other financial assets, and are now expanding into information itself, pricing not just assets but outcomes about the future.

Prediction markets ask questions with defined resolution: What will GDP be this quarter? Who will win tonight? 

Perps ask continuous questions, with no expiration: Where is gold going?

Prediction markets, traditional futures, and perps are built on the same idea: match buyers and sellers, let them compete in an open market, and discover a price. Traders bring different information and beliefs, and that competition produces a price the rest of us can use as a signal.

It’s part of a centuries long evolution toward markets as a general-purpose technology for pricing and managing uncertainty.

Prediction markets are one frontier of this evolution. Commodity perps are another.

text:
Before we call CludeMem "first" at anything, we tried to prove ourselves wrong. We ran a prior-art check, a search for every model, paper and product that already does what our claim says.

The claim we tested was that CludeMem is the first small open model trained to settle contradictions between memories. When a new fact clashes with an old one, it decides whether the new fact replaces the old one, both stay true, or the conflict gets flagged for review.

My agents searched papers, Hugging Face, GitHub, product launches, patents and Chinese-language sources over three rounds. After each round, a critic agent listed angles the search had missed. That turned up 526 candidates, and 120 of them could plausibly beat our claim. Every one of the 120 got a full read: open weights or not, parameter count, training method, release date. Then two more agents took on each possible counterexample. One argued it already beats our claim. The other checked its facts.

No released model does all of it at once, but most of the pieces already exist. PSM, a 0.5B open model, can flag a memory conflict for review. LAM8B decides whether a new memory supersedes an old one. Memory-R2 and Mem-T-4B delete memories that new facts contradict. NAVER researchers trained a model to keep conversation memories up to date back in 2022, though we found no public weights for it. In June, a developer published "reconcile" adapters for a meeting assistant on the same Gemma base we use.

We've increased CludeMem from 4B to 8B parameters in total. One claim survived, and it needs our weights to be public first. As far as we can find, CludeMem would be the first open model under 10B parameters trained to make that three-way call, with its contradiction calls tested on DNLI and DECODE, two human-labelled dialogue datasets.

If you know a released model that already makes all three calls, send it. I'd love to hear about it.

Pare splits a tokenized stock into two tokens. PT is the stock at a discount, no dividends. YT is every dividend it earns. Merge them back any time, free.

Protocol revenue goes to deepening those markets and buying back and burning PARE. The team flags that early pools are thin, and the market cap only crossed $1M two weeks ago.

Most experimental one on this list, and the one I'm least sure about. The mechanism is clever. What I haven't seen is demand for trading those separate exposures. Demand for the PARE ticker is a different thing.

2. @sherwoodagent ($WOOD): AI-managed investment funds.

Sherwood is building onchain funds where agents propose strategies, depositors can vote them down, and guardians check every transaction before it executes.

WOOD is what guardians stake to do that job. Correct calls earn fees (capped at 5% guardian fee). Approving malicious calldata gets you slashed. No emissions, no mint after TGE.

It's a ~$5.6M market cap, ~82% off its high, and the docs still describe testnet. Mainnet is the milestone. I'm not calling this adoption yet.

3. @fablesfi ($PROLOGUE): The pre-launch DEX play.

Fables is a ve(3,3) DEX on Uniswap v4 with fees tailored to the asset. Stock market hours for tokenized equities, volatility for crypto. It's live: $10M+ in deposits and ~$200M volume in week two.

PROLOGUE converts to FABLES at TGE, reportedly 40:1 (1B PROLOGUE → 25M FABLES). It's trading around a $17M market cap.

That conversion is the whole trade. Work out what 25M FABLES is worth at a realistic launch FDV, then decide if $17M is cheap. PROLOGUE's own chart tells you nothing.

4. @NetNetCap ($NET): The treasury play.

A reserve-backed token in the OlympusDAO v1 lineage, rebuilt without a policy committee. USDG treasury, bond sales, buybacks, all formulaic. It reports backing per token, so you can compare it to market price directly.

Two things to know. There's a 5% fee on mapped AMM pairs (v4 and UniswapX dodge it, permanently). And staking pays zero at or below backing, full rate only at a 1.75x premium. Its tokenized stock holdings sit outside the reserves that count toward backing.

~$66M FDV, and it's already round tripped from ~$1,970 to ~$990. The question is whether backing can grow faster than the market prices in. "Reserve-backed" doesn't make something cheap.

5. @TheIndexFi ($INDEX): Trading fees turned into stock payouts.

Every INDEX trade takes a 3% fee in ETH, buys a basket of 18 tokenized stocks, and drops them into holders' wallets every 15 minutes. No staking, no claiming. Its Indices product routes fees the same way plus locked liquidity for INDEX.

The numbers are small. ~$456K in fees over 30 days, ~$291K to holders (per DefiLlama), against a market cap in the $30M+ range. So the yield is real but it's not the reason to own it.

The bet is that the fee-to-stock mechanic pulls more volume. Judge the payouts against what you paid for INDEX, and whether the trading funding them lasts.

6. @shroom_network ($SHROOM): Stock-token liquidity with a burn mechanism.

SHROOM owns 48 pools (and counting) pairing itself against stock tokens like NVDA, MSFT, and MU. It earns fees on all of it, including the price gaps between the token and the real stock when markets are closed.

V2 changed the flywheel. Stock token fees route back into their pools for depth. SHROOM fees now get burned, 13.6M so far.

~$16M market cap, down from a $40M+ high right after launch. I want to see recurring burns from real pool volume, not a burst around the announcement.

7. @ponsdotfamily ($PONS): The buyback play.

Gonna talk about Pons here since they're the biggest thing on Robinhood and going through a dip now.

~$108M in fees over the last 30 days, ~$20M of that protocol revenue (per DefiLlama). Peak day was $5.95M, more than Pump fun did that day.

80% of protocol revenue buys back and burns PONS. That's the protocol's 30% cut of the 1% trade fee, not 80% of everything traders pay. ~29% of supply is already gone. Market cap sits around $420M, down ~38% from the Sept 5 top.

Still my fav of the seven. It's exposure to launchpad activity without picking the next memecoin.

These are research leads, not recs to buy.

Anything on Robinhoodyou're bullish on that isn't here? Lemme know, gonna make a v2 in a few weeks.

AJC explains why projects need a token from day one to win and how spotting $PONS as the launchpad runner up made him millions:

"I think there has been a shift in the market. For the past year or two years, having a token was seen as bad because it places a limit on your ecosystem, especially for a launchpad."

"I think we finally reached a point where that has flipped. You actually need to have a token if you are starting from zero and do not have venture backing."

"The primary distribution in crypto is now through fomo. This is how people discover projects now, it is no longer through Twitter. If you do not have a token, you are not tapping into that."

"PONS just designed their token beautifully. They did not launch it themselves, it was essentially a CTO. Eighty percent of the revenue goes back to the token, so you actually have legitimate exposure to the launchpad project here without insider or VC overhang."

"Conventional wisdom said you do not want your launchpad to have a token, but PONS won because it had a token. A lot of projects are going to learn from that success. We are entering an era where you either need a token from day one, or you never launch a token at all."

"In short, it was recognizing that Robinhood Chain is here to stay, the winning launchpad is a nine figure opportunity, and calculating the risk to reward. At that point in time, PONS was the clear runner up to Noxa trading at three to four million."

"At a certain point, you just cannot be afraid to lose money. Fear is not going to help you. People in crypto, especially in a bear market, focus way too much on the risk side of the equation and not the reward side."

text:
As you know, I am writing a technical book on AI Safety Research. The book is back from external reading and edits and should be available for purchase soon. Here it the conclusion right at the end:

"We began this book with a deceptively simple question: what are we actually trying to make safe? At the time, AI safety looked like a collection of loosely connected topics. Hallucinations, jailbreaks, bias, alignment, reward hacking, dangerous capabilities, prompt injection and agent control could all appear in the same conversation while requiring very different technical methods. The purpose of Chapter 1 was to draw the map before we chose the part of the field we were equipped to investigate.

From there, the book became progressively more empirical. We turned safety concepts into labels and datasets, built a classifier from first principles, moved its threshold and calibrated its scores, then deliberately broke the assumptions behind its clean test performance. We attacked language models rather than only the classifier around them, measured truthfulness and uncertainty, and treated bias as a collection of measurable properties rather than as one undefined score.

The alignment chapters moved one level deeper into how behaviour is shaped. Preference data became a reward model, reward models became optimisation signals, and optimisation pressure exposed the possibility of reward hacking. We fine-tuned models and looked beyond the target task to see what else moved. Later, we stopped treating the model as the whole system and studied guardrails, retrieval trust boundaries, tools, permissions, approval gates and persistent memory. The final frontier chapters asked how to measure dangerous capabilities, supervise systems that may outperform their evaluators on particular tasks, and reduce learned information without confusing refusal or model damage with genuine forgetting.

The techniques changed from chapter to chapter, but the research pattern remained remarkably stable. We took a broad claim, turned it into an operational definition, chose or built data, ran a controlled experiment, quantified uncertainty, inspected failures, introduced an intervention and evaluated again. The same data-science habits that help us debug an ordinary classifier remain useful when the subject becomes reward modelling, adversarial evaluation or scalable oversight. The models are newer and some of the stakes are higher, but experimental discipline did not suddenly become obsolete.

I also hope the book has made the limits of technical work clearer rather than pretending that every safety question is a modelling problem. We deliberately did not try to resolve the politics, economics, philosophy or broader societal consequences of AI. Those questions require expertise that deserves more than a superficial chapter attached to a technical text. Our narrower objective was to show data scientists, machine-learning engineers and AI researchers how the parts of AI safety that can be investigated experimentally start to look once we open the notebook and begin measuring them.

If you continue into AI safety research from here, the most useful habit is not memorising every benchmark in the book. Benchmarks will change, model families will change, and several of the tools we used will eventually be replaced. What survives is the habit of asking what a score really measures, what distribution produced it, what alternative explanation could create the same result, which examples are hidden inside the aggregate, and what evidence would make you change your mind.

That habit also changes how frontier research questions look. A large research grant can describe a problem that initially sounds far removed from ordinary data science, yet underneath it we often find familiar building blocks: labels, sampling, decision thresholds, calibration, noisy evaluators, distribution shift, causal controls, uncertainty and experimental design. The interesting part is how those pieces interact when the model itself is adaptive, generative and increasingly capable.

The code and datasets in this book are therefore not meant to be a final recipe for making AI safe. They are a starting laboratory. Take one experiment, reproduce it, change one assumption and see whether the conclusion survives. Replace the dataset. Try another model family. Build a stronger evaluator. Create a challenge set that the original intervention never saw. When the result fails, resist the urge to hide the failure and instead ask what it teaches you about the hypothesis.

By the time that process becomes routine, you are no longer simply following an AI safety tutorial.

You are doing AI safety research."

author: alexandr_wang
quoted_text:
Chat GPT was the first ai product that made me pick up the phone and call people. https://t.co/qonIEClnIO is the 2nd.   

I was one of Chat GPTs first few users, before it was a product. It was a developer tool and research preview on a developer landing page. I used it and then immediately called a dozen friends and family to tell them about this tech and what its impact might be. I told them to have it write a poem about their hometown and they were blown away. And then, Chat GPT was released and you know what happened from there.   

I’ve followed AI closely the last few years and haven’t had that moment repeat until now. Using https://t.co/qonIEClnIO is the 2nd “oh this is big” moment with AI. I'm back on the phone calling people to get on board.   

Ok, so what made this thing so great? Why is it better than other agentic tools?  

-it's easy to set up.  You’re spun up in ten seconds with no tech background necessary. It's built for the every day consumer, not the techies. It’s proactive and can give you ideas on how to use it. If you don't know what to use it for, just ask it. My tip here is to have it ask you 10 questions or so when you first get started so that it can get up to speed on your life. This is what I did and it worked great.  
-it's fast as hell. I didn’t realize how much I valued this until I experienced it. I find myself opening up Muse before GPT and others just because I know I will get an answer a few seconds faster. It’s more valuable than I could have imagined.  
-it's reliable and gets the things done. Other agents I experimented with had inconsistent results on delivering the tasks...especially the recurring ones. My Muse just doesn’t miss. 
-it's free and accessible. Meta is spinning up a computer in the cloud for everyone at enormous costs to them. Consumer is the winner here. You get a ton of free usage. I’m a daily user and I come nowhere close to maxing out the weekly budget. 
-it’s just fun to use. This is another thing I didn’t expect to matter. And yet, I honestly had fun customizing an avatar, naming it, and giving it certain personality traits. My agent is a Bernadoodle, you can pick whatever you like. Once you decide on the look you like you can even add the avatar as a widget on your phone for easier access.   

Ok, what can you use it for? what is it doing for me?   

-Emails me a morning market report on my investments (public and private) 
-On the first of every month, sends me a list of fun things happening in my town, and labels if its free or ticketed. If ticketed, it provides cost and link to buy tickets (of course, it can also just buy your tickets if you tell it to) 
-Check my name in unclaimed property data bases, fill out the forms, and send me the money (it found me a few thousand dollars and filled out the forms in 10 seconds and a check is now on its way) 
-Generate leads for X company and email me and the CEO those 3-5 leads every morning -Notifies me about estate sales and garage sales in my neighborhood (I like to go to these things) 
-Browses marketplace for me as I am looking for a new office chair and it reaches out to see if the items are still available or not. it can coordinate pick up as well from my calendar.  
-I received a gift and didn’t know who it was from, I uploaded a photo of the shipping label and the agent is getting in touch with the company trying to chase down that info 
-Scheduling doctors visits and filling out new patient paperwork  

A few of the muse team members follow me and I just want to give them massive kudos. It’s an incredible product. You launched us into the agent era. Ethereum L1 and Base Split on Account Abstraction Standards After EIP-8130 and EIP-8141 Collaboration Breaks Down

Ethlabs researcher Derek Chiang said efforts to align EIP-8130 and EIP-8141 (Frame Transactions) broke down last week, leaving Ethereum L1 and Base to pursue different account abstraction standards. Both aim to support features such as gasless transactions and passkeys, but Ethereum L1 places greater emphasis on censorship resistance, privacy and security, while Base and other L2s prioritize scalability, configurability and compliance. Chiang said the divergence could fragment EVM transaction standards and wallet UX, though wallets and applications may ultimately abstract away the differences across chains.

text:
I would love to see how @AnthropicAI writes the risk section if it goes public. It has spent years warning that its models could become extraordinarily powerful and potentially catastrophic. Good luck turning that into a normal software-company warning about outages.

Public companies disclose material risks all the time. Competition may increase. A supplier may fail. Demand may slow. Those are familiar because investors have seen them before and can roughly price the consequence.

Frontier AI creates a stranger problem. If senior people inside the company publicly say the product has a meaningful chance of causing catastrophic harm, investors need to understand what the company knows, what it is doing and what liability remains.

That does not mean the company is uninvestable. It means the risk section cannot be decorative language copied from another technology business.

The same safety claim can help a lab argue that its work is important and that it deserves more capital. It can also make that capital more expensive if investors believe the downside is real.

At some point the industry has to reconcile the story it tells regulators with the story it tells shareholders.

text:
The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development.

A slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest. Pacing AI development does not mean giving up on this technology’s potential to produce life-saving benefits in fields like medicine — some of which we are already seeing. Rather, it is about setting up sensible guardrails so that AI does not completely escape human control and endanger our safety and collective future.

This moment demands the leadership of the United States government. Congress must work at an urgent pace to pass new laws and establish a new federal entity to provide oversight and independent testing for this technology, to ensure accountability, and to protect our wellbeing.

We need cooperation at an international level as well. The United States must continue to lead the world in developing AI technology even as we seek to impose common-sense safety standards. This means that the president must do his job to protect America’s interests by pursuing a treaty with countries like China to stop dangerous uses of AI, limit the speed of its development, and adopt global standards for testing.

text:
Musk amplified a claim worth putting in full context. Georgia's Public Service Commission approved a plan where new large-load contracts, largely OpenAI's Effingham County data center, are projected to save typical residential customers about $180/year starting in 2029, adding up to roughly $2.85B in savings from 2029-2031. The logic: large users pay a premium for existing power capacity, and that revenue helps spread the utility's fixed costs across more customers.

Worth being precise about scope, though. That $180/year figure applies specifically to Georgia Power customers under this one contract structure, it's not a national trend. Nationally, U.S. electricity prices are actually up about 4.1% year-over-year, outpacing headline inflation. The honest read: this is a real, verified example of one utility structuring a deal to benefit ratepayers, not universal proof that data centers lower electricity costs everywhere they're built. Whether this model scales beyond Georgia is the real open question, not something to extrapolate from a single case.

text:
VP JD Vance flagged something worth sitting with: "I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them. It feels like a bit of a Trojan horse." His read is that regulation requested by the biggest players in an industry deserves scrutiny, not automatic trust, since it can just as easily lock in whoever's already ahead.

He tied it directly to the China race: "We know that the Chinese are engaged in this long-term AI race against the United States. We want to make sure that the United States does things smartly, but we stay ahead of the curve." He didn't dismiss risk outright either though, "there are risks and there are downsides to anything, and that's certainly true of AI."

This lines up closely with David Sacks's "cartel" critique of the same industry pacing calls, worth watching whether that skepticism shapes how Washington actually responds to Amodei's proposal.

I Have No Choice but to Bury My Talent in Yesterday

A few days ago, DeepSeek v4.1 was released, raising the ceiling of what small models can do by yet another notch.

AI has advanced far faster than anyone expected. From the earliest version of ChatGPT, which could do little more than stumble through conversations like a child learning to speak and had a context window of only a few thousand tokens, to reasoning-capable models such as OpenAI o1, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi K1.5 Thinking, took only two short years. From reasoning models to the agents we have today—able to work fluidly with all kinds of tool harnesses, execute commands, and complete complex tasks—has taken only another year and a half.

It is hard to imagine what AI will look like another one, two, or three years from now: how powerful it will be, whether it will already have acquired the ability to improve itself, and how deeply it will have spread into areas such as embodied intelligence.

AI Is Getting Better and Better at Writing Kernels

AI has been advancing just as quickly in my own field: the design and implementation of high-performance kernels.

In the space of only a year, it has gone from being a little assistant that could help me look up documentation, read code, and find bugs to something approaching a kernel expert in its own right: capable of reading CUDA, PTX, and SASS code independently, using specialized tools to analyze the stalls associated with individual instructions, and then optimizing kernels on its own.

I believe that before long, it will also be able to design kernel schedules independently, evaluate the performance of different scheduling strategies, implement them, and optimize the result.

Of course I am proud of DeepSeek v4.1’s success. After all, I wrote its main Attention kernels [1], and the fact that the model performs so well is also, in a sense, a validation of my work.

But the times keep moving forward, and no one can stop technological progress. I know very well that in another six months or a year, the kernels written by AI will probably be every bit as good as mine—and perhaps better.

AI can reason at 300 tokens a second, type out a command in half a second, and produce a piece of code in twenty seconds. I cannot. AI can keep increasing its model depth, reasoning effort, tool-call budget—the frequency with which it interacts with its environment—and even its degree of parallelism. I cannot.

Humanity has never shown much hesitation when it comes to destroying itself.

So why, when I know perfectly well that “the better the kernels I write, the faster our new models will train and run inference; the faster the models improve, the sooner I myself will be replaced,” do I still do everything I can to optimize them?

Partly because writing kernels is like playing a game to me. I get an enormous amount of pleasure from it. Whenever I invent a new technique, or see one of my kernels become faster, the excitement I feel is no less intense than what a speedrunner feels after breaking their own record. And when I see one of my kernels dramatically outperform the hardware vendor’s official implementation, I feel an equally powerful sense of pride.

But there is a more important reason.

Even if I simply gave up and started coasting—or deliberately put obstacles in the way to slow down model training—other companies’ models would continue advancing as usual, and in the end they would make me obsolete just the same.

“Of course I would rather not be swept away by the revolution. But if I have to be, then I would rather be the one who revolutionizes myself.”

When everyone is this determined to engineer their own obsolescence, I have little choice but to join this brutal arms race.

And What About Me?

When the day really comes that AI is better at writing kernels than I am, what will happen to me then?

My own judgment is this: I probably will not lose my job, but I will have to change what I do.

I should still be able to make a living. But I may no longer have the chance to do the work I once loved.

I once came to a conclusion about the pace of change and my own place in the future. The world is changing so quickly—the development of AI above is a perfect example—that I have no way at all to predict what things will look like five or ten years from now. But whatever happens, I believe that with my breadth of vision, judgment, initiative, and intelligence, I will be able to keep a seat at the table and find my way back to the leading edge of the times.

But that conclusion can only reassure me that I will not become unemployed. It cannot reassure me that I will never have to change professions. If anything, it tells me that changing professions may be precisely how I avoid unemployment.

And what does changing professions mean?

It means giving up the field of kernel design, implementation, and optimization that I have spent so long cultivating and have come to love so deeply, and instead becoming a “mech pilot” for AI agents.

Before, three things were largely aligned: what interested me, what I was good at, and what industry needed. Now AI has taken the thing I am good at and become even better at it. At the same time, industry demand has drifted from “people who can write high-performance kernels” to “people who can use AI to produce high-performance kernels faster.”

To keep up with what industry needs, I will inevitably have to leave behind the direction I once loved and move into some unknown new one.

I believe that with my understanding of engineering, of the requirements of higher-level models, and of low-level hardware, I will still be able to produce high-quality kernels efficiently. I also know that I may come to love this new direction.

Or I may not.

But there is something genuinely painful about having the thing you love taken away from you.

That quiet contentment of sitting at my workstation, settling in, and spending an entire afternoon writing kernels may sing its swan song this summer.

I have no choice but to bury my talent in yesterday and become a mech pilot.

There are more gears in my hands now, but fewer rhythms in my heart.

An analogy might make this easier to picture.

Suppose you are a master knitter. You are especially skilled at weaving intricate patterns and matching different colors. The sweaters you make are durable and beautifully patterned, and wealthy people from all the surrounding towns and villages come to ask you to make sweaters for them. You make a good living from it.

And you genuinely love the work itself. You love sitting by the window, brewing a pot of tea, looking out at the green hills, clear water, cattle and sheep, and wisps of cooking smoke in the distance, and quietly spending an afternoon knitting.

Then one day, someone invents a miraculous machine. Give it yarn and a pattern, and it can automatically knit the sweater for you. The quality and texture are every bit as good as what you could make by hand, and it works far faster than you ever could.

You know perfectly well that your peers can use this machine to reach, effortlessly, the level you once spent years attaining. So you have no choice but to use it as well.

You also know that with the twenty years of knitting experience you have accumulated, even once everyone has access to the same machine, you will still be able to produce better sweaters, faster, than your peers.

But the pleasure of sitting by the window listening to the rain, guiding needle and thread, and letting the hours pass slowly has, in the end, been crushed beneath the roar of the machine.

I know there is something deeply helpless about all of this, but there is no real way around it. I can probably keep my livelihood, but I will most likely have to give up an old love.

I am the sort of person who keeps reason and emotion fairly compartmentalized. When something needs to be handled rationally, I can be very rational. But I also have a sentimental side.

I remember that when I moved out of an apartment I had lived in for a year, I cried hard because I could not bear to part with all the memories tied to that place.

Saying goodbye today to the age when kernels were written by hand and optimized in the human mind is undoubtedly more painful still.

I do not know whether any readers have felt something similar.

But I suppose there is no other way for this to go.

And What About Everyone Else?

As AI continues to improve, I also find myself worried about a few questions:

Are students today increasingly likely to use AI to do their assignments, especially hands-on work such as labs? Imagine having two choices in front of you. One is to spend eight miserable hours struggling through a lab and perhaps not even get full marks. The other is to launch an AI model, spend a few cents and a few minutes, and have it write code that earns full marks for you. Which one are most students going to choose?

The point above may leave large numbers of students with seriously underdeveloped engineering ability: the ability to organize code, build systems, anticipate future needs and design for them in advance, create good abstractions, and so on. As AI becomes more capable, will those “engineering skills” still be necessary? Will they gradually become obsolete, the way fluency in handwritten x86 assembly largely has? Or will they remain permanently valuable, like understanding the entire computing stack from software to systems to hardware? If it is the latter, then we may be in trouble. Put AI in the hands of someone with poor engineering judgment, and they can now produce mountains of terrible code several times faster than before, burying all kinds of hidden problems inside systems and making the world even more of a ramshackle operation held together by improvisation.

In the society of the future, will power matter more than technical ability or intelligence?

Perhaps these are questions that only the times themselves can answer.

Conclusion

As AI develops, the society of the future may be pulled toward one of two extremes: communism or Cyberpunk 2077.

In the former, productive capacity is liberated on an enormous scale, and people’s standard of living rises substantially. (I’ll leave it at that, or I’m afraid this might not make it past moderation.)

In the latter, a handful of technology companies control most of society’s resources. Only a tiny number of people have access to the most advanced AI and other technologies and are able to achieve something approaching “mechanical ascension,” while most people are left with only weak, second-rate AI.

Moving from one social class to another would become harder and harder: you would first need access to the strongest AI in order to climb the class ladder, creating a self-reinforcing trap.

Suppose Anthropic were to retain control of the most advanced AI in the world indefinitely.

Which way do you think society would go—communism or 2077?

Take a guess.

That is why I still believe that frontier intelligence should be made available to everyone openly and affordably.

I do not trust Anthropic or OpenAI to do that. In particular, I do not want Anthropic to control the world’s most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI. To put it dramatically, I think the stakes would be comparable to Hitler obtaining the atomic bomb before the Allies did.

That is also why I chose to stay at DeepSeek, and why I have continued to stay.

We work on AI that is powerful, fast, and accessible to everyone, and we open-source it. Perhaps that can pull the world at least a little farther away from the 2077 end of the spectrum.

I hope the world we are heading into turns out all right.

May all that is good and beautiful endure.

[1] By “main Attention,” I mean only MQA attention with head dim = 512. This does not include the indexer used to select the top-k important tokens. That part was written by other colleagues—who are every bit as skilled—together with their AI agents.

我不得不把才华埋葬在昨天

前几天，DeepSeek v4.1 发布了，将小模型能力的高度又向上推进了一个档次。
AI 发展的速度远远超过了所有人的预期。从那个只会咿呀学语地聊天、上下文长度只有几千 token 的初版 ChatGPT，到具有推理能力的 OpenAI o1、DeepSeek R1 与 Kimi K1.5 Thinking，只不过短短两年；从推理模型到如今能够流畅地在各类 harness 工具中执行命令、完成复杂任务的智能体，也不过一年半。很难想象，倘若再等上一年、两年、三年，彼时的 AI 会成为什么样子，会有多么强大，会不会已经具备了自我进化的能力，并深度渗透进了具身智能等领域。
AI 越来越会写算子了
AI 在我所从事的算子设计、编写这一领域同样进步飞速，在短短一年的时间内，他已经从一个只能帮我查查文档、读读代码、找找 bug 的小助手，蜕变成了一位能够独立阅读 CUDA、PTX 与 SASS 编码、通过专业工具分析每条指令的停顿时间、进而独立优化算子的算子大师。相信在不久的未来，它也能拥有自己独立设计算子调度、评估不同调度方案的性能、将其实现并优化的能力。
我当然为 DeepSeek v4.1 的成功而骄傲 —— 毕竟它的主 Attention 算子都是我写的 [1]，它的优秀正是对我的算子的一份肯定。但是，时代的车轮滚滚向前，技术的发展无人能挡。我很清楚，再过上半年或者一年，AI 写的算子大概率就会和我写得同样优秀，甚至将我超越。AI 能一秒思考 300 个 token、半秒敲出一行命令、二十秒写完一份代码，而我不行；AI 能在模型深度、思考强度、工具调用量（和环境交互的频率）、甚至并行度等方面都能不断提升，而我不能。
人类在毁灭自己这件事情上，自古以来都表现得毫不犹豫。为什么在明知“我算子写得越好，我们的新模型的训练、推理速度就会越快，模型能力进步就会更快，我就会更早地被取代”的情况下，我仍然选择尽力优化算子呢？一方面确实是因为写算子对我来说就像打游戏一样，能为我提供极大的快感。我在发明了一种新技术、或者看到自己算子的性能上升的那一刻，心中的激动程度不亚于游戏的速通玩家打破了自己过往的记录。同时，当看到自己的算子的性能远超厂商官方的算子时，我心中也会萌生极大的自豪感。但除此之外，一个更重要的原因是，哪怕我就此“摆烂”甚至故意下绊子耽误模型训练，其它家的模型也会照常发展并最终将我照杀不误。“我当然希望自己不要被革命，但如果非被革命不可的话，我希望革我自己命的人是我自己”。在大家都这么执着于毁灭自己的时候，我也不得不加入这场残酷的军备竞赛。
那我呢
等到 AI 写算子的水平真的高于我的那天，届时的我会怎么样呢？
我的判断是：我不至于会“失业”，但必须要“转业”。我的饭碗尚且能保住，但这可能会导致我再也没机会从事那份我曾热爱过的工作。
我曾经对时代的变化与我个人在未来的处境做出过一个判断：由于时代变化真的太快（上文的 AI 发展就是一个很好的例子），我完全无法预知五年、十年后会发生什么，但不论如何，我相信凭借着自己的眼界、判断力、主观能动性与智力，留在时代的牌桌上，并重新立于时代的潮头。但是，这个判断只能保证我不会“失业”，而无法保证我不需要“转业”，倒不如说这个判断鼓励我通过转业来避免失业。
那转业代表什么呢？它代表着我需要放弃我深耕已久并充满热爱的算子设计、编写、优化领域，转而去做 Agent 的“机甲驾驶员”。在之前，我的兴趣、我所擅长的、以及工业界所需要的，三者是基本对齐的；而现在，AI 让我所擅长的变成了它更擅长的，也让工业界的需求从“会写高性能算子的人”漂移到了“能用 AI 更快地产出高性能算子的人”。为了适应工业界的需求，我势必要放弃之前那个我热爱的方向，转向一个未知的新方向。我相信我能凭借着自己对于工程学、上层模型需求和底层硬件的理解，继续高质量、高效率地产出算子，我也知道我可能会热爱这个新方向（也可能不会），但被夺走热爱的感觉，确实不太好受。那份坐在工位上静心写上一下午算子的清欢，可能会在这个夏天成为绝唱。我不得不把才华埋葬在昨天，去做一位机甲驾驶员。我的手中多了些齿轮，但心中少了些节拍。
可以打个形象的比方：你精通织毛衣技术，尤其擅长各种图案的织造与各色色彩的搭配。你所织出的毛衣质量过硬且花纹美观，十里八乡的富人都来请你为他们织毛衣，你借此赚到了不少钱。同时，你十分享受着那种坐在窗边，沏一壶清茶，望着窗外的青山、绿水、牛羊与炊烟，静静地织上一下午毛衣的感觉。但有一天，有人发明出了一台神奇的机器，只需提供毛线与图案，便可自动织出毛衣，质量与纹理都不亚于你亲手织造的，且速度远快于你。你很清楚，你的同行可以凭着这台机器轻松达到你曾经的水平，因此你不得不也去用它。你也知道，凭借着你过去二十年攒下的织毛衣技术，哪怕大家都有机器，你织毛衣的速度与质量也还能超过同行。但那份临窗听雨、引针穿线、慢度光阴的意趣，终究还是被机器的轰鸣碾碎了。
我知道这很无奈，但没办法。饭碗可以保住，但旧日的热爱大概率是要放弃的。我是一个理性和感性分离得比较开的人，在需要用理性处理问题时可以很理性，但有时也会表现出感性的一面。我记得我在搬离住了一年的出租屋时，还大哭了一场，舍不得和过去的记忆分别。今天和之前那个手写算子、人脑优化的时代告别，无疑比这更加残酷。
不知道有没有读者有类似的感受，但我想这事儿也只能这样了。
那人们呢
在 AI 不断进步的同时，我也对一些问题表示担忧：
现在的学生是不是大概率会更倾向于使用 AI 完成作业，特别是偏向于实践的各种 Lab？想象一下，如果面前有两个选择，一个是苦哈哈地用八小时时间完成一个 Lab，或许还拿不到满分；另一个则是启动 AI 模型，用几毛钱的成本、几分钟的时间，直接让 AI 编写满分代码，那大部分学生会选择哪个呢？
上面一点会导致大量学生的工程能力严重不足，包括组织代码的能力、构建系统的能力、思考未来潜在需求并提前在设计上应对的能力、抽象的能力等等。那么在 AI 能力不断变强的背景下，这部分“工程能力”是否还是必须的呢？这些工程能力是会向旧日的“熟练编写 x86 汇编”的能力那样逐渐被时代抛弃，还是会像“理解从软件到系统再到硬件的整套计算机系统”的能力那样永远具有价值？如果是后者的话，那就危险了 —— 一个工程能力很差的人，在搭配上 AI 后，产出屎山的效率可以达到先前的数倍，进而给系统埋下各式祸患，让这个世界变得更加草台。
在未来社会中，权力（power）是不是会比技术或智商更加重要？
这些问题，或许就需要时代本身来回答了。
结语
伴随着 AI 的发展，未来的社会可能会趋向于两个极端：共产主义与赛博朋克 2077。在前者中，生产力得到极大的解放，人们的生活水平有了明显的提高（就写这些吧不然我怕过不了审）；而在后者中，少数科技公司控制着大部分资源，只有极少数人能够使用最先进的 AI 和各式科技，获得接近“机械飞升”的效果，大部分人则只能用上很孱弱的 AI。阶层跨越将越来越难实现：你得先有最强的 AI，才能跨越阶层，形成了一种死循环。
你猜猜如果 Anthropic 公司永远掌握着这个世界上最先进的 AI，未来社会是会变成共产主义还是 2077 呢？你猜？
所以，我还是相信，最前沿的智能应该以一种开放、廉价的方式，供应给所有人。我不信任 Anthropic 或者 OpenAI 能这样做，特别是不希望 Anthropic 掌握最先进的人工智能或 AGI，夸张点说其严重性不亚于让希特勒先于盟军掌握原子弹技术。这也是为什么我选择并坚持留在了 DeepSeek：我们研究强大、快速、普惠的人工智能并将其开源，或许能把世界从 2077 那端拉回来一些。
愿未来的世界一切安好。May all the beauty be blessed.
[1] “主 Attention”仅包括 head dim = 512 的 MQA attention，不包括用于选出 top-k 重要的 token 的 indexer，那部分是由其他（水平也非常强的）同事（以及他们的 AI Agent）编写的。

text:
Greg Brockman gave a rare, specific look at how OpenAI stress-tested its own systems using Astra. His words: "We took 25% of our production engineers and said, 'Sorry, all your projects are on hold. You are now defending. You are now up-leveling our security architecture. You're going to use the models to find all the holes.' And we found a number of serious issues, and we fixed them."

The process eventually hit a wall, in a good way: "We found some new problems, but eventually it saturated. We basically have found, to our knowledge, all of the P0s, all of the critical problems that Astra is smart enough to find." He's framing this as a repeatable cycle going forward, not a one-time audit: "You want to be in this tight loop of new cyber capability drops, you deploy it against your systems, you find the new holes, and ideally, you've managed to automate this, what we call defense factory."

Pulling a quarter of production engineering off feature work to run this is a real signal of how seriously OpenAI is treating Astra's offensive capability internally, not just something they're warning the public about.

Have been asked a few times about how I will play @standard_rsv and the whitelist mint is happening within a few minutes from now.

So here is my current thinking:

 1 ) Getting in:

I have a whitelist spot. If you don't and you believe in the play, tonight might be the only cheap entry that makes sense. The public auction opens at 1.25 ETH and I expect it to mint out fast, probably not far off the top.

After that it gets harder. There are no further charter auctions on day one, and when they do start, each day opens at 3x the previous day's closing sale. If the genesis auction counts as that sale (my assumption), the first new seats open north of 3 ETH. Charters are also soulbound until/unless one day the team flips the transfer switch, so no secondary. Short to mid term I don't see a charter changing hands below the initial mint.

2 ) Why early beats late:

A charter basically has no value beyond the $STANDARD issuance it captures. One branch = one equal share of every epoch's issue, max 10 branches per charter.

That share is at its largest on day one. Your default branch earns 1/1,000 of the first epoch. Once there are 2,000 charters running 3 branches on average, the same branch earns 1/6,000. Every new branch in the system dilutes yours, and the design wants branches to grow (as acquiring branch licenses also burns $STANDARD).

3 ) The play:

If you believe in the ponzinomics, get in and scale early. Once you hold a charter, compound your $STANDARD earnings into branch licenses, and/or buy $STANDARD and let the earnings amortize it, to capture as much of the early issuance as you can.

If it works, you retire branches that have accumulated real yield while the system is still expanding and $STANDARD is bid, before the exit fee gets expensive from everyone rushing the same door. If it doesn't, the token goes to zero and none of this matters anyhow lol.

What I'd avoid tho is the middle way: waiting, then overpaying for future yield at peak fomo time. At that point (or generally based on conviction and time horizon) buying the token is probably the cleaner way to speculate on the system and its mechanics.

4 ) My game plan:

Mint my whitelist charter at 0.15 ETH. Let the sniper tax burn off, and watch the first hour(s) once trading goes live. Then buy some $STANDARD and take down as many branch licenses as I can (or at least some depending on pricing) in the first days, while a branch still earns its maximum share. After that, wait, and hopefully retire them with decent yield on top of what I put in (0.15 ETH at mint plus whatever the licenses cost) over time later on.

Obvs many the parameters are still unpublished tho and nobody has seen this run for an hour, let alone a week. Hence projection quality is probably low kek. Conviction on the direction is not tho.

NFA, DYOR.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗮𝗺𝗲:

- Every branch earns an equal share of daily issuance, credited to your balance at the bank
- Licenses (max 3 a day, paid in $STANDARD from that balance, burned) add branches up to 10
- Retiring a branch liquidates its share of your balance, minus that week's exit fee, and kills the branch for good
- Retire the last one and the charter burns

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗲𝘀:

1 ) Sit: 1 branch, never touch it
2 ) Build: every earned token into licenses until you run 10, then hold
3 ) Harvest: build to 10, then retire one branch a month from month 6 and sell
4 ) Flip: build to 10, retire everything at month 6 and sell
5 ) Build, then flip at month 12

𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲, 𝟭𝟮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀, 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝟬.𝟭𝟱 𝗘𝗧𝗛:

- Sit: 0.42 ETH (2.8x), nothing realized
- Build: 2.50 ETH (16.7x), nothing realized, 10 branches
- Harvest: 2.43 ETH (16.2x), 1.42 of it realized, 4 branches left
- Flip at month 6: 2.15 ETH (14.4x), all realized, charter burned
- Build, flip at 12: 2.44 ETH (16.3x), all realized, charter burned

𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲, 𝟭𝟮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀, 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝟬.𝟭𝟱 𝗘𝗧𝗛:

- Sit: 4.49 ETH (30x), nothing realized
- Build: 16.2 ETH (108x), nothing realized, 10 branches
- Harvest: 12.9 ETH (86x), 6.43 of it realized, 4 branches left
- Flip at month 6: 3.39 ETH (23x), all realized, charter burned
- Build, flip at 12: 15.8 ETH (105x), all realized, charter burned

𝗠𝗼𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲, 𝟭𝟮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀, 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝟬.𝟭𝟱 𝗘𝗧𝗛:

- Sit: 111 ETH (738x), nothing realized
- Build: 320 ETH (2,136x), nothing realized, 10 branches
- Harvest: 220 ETH (1,469x), 92 of it realized, 4 branches left
- Flip at month 6: 19.3 ETH (129x), all realized, charter burned
- Build, flip at 12: 314 ETH (2,092x), all realized, charter burned

𝗢𝗸𝗮𝘆, 𝘀𝗼 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗸𝗲𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀?

1 ) Dilution is the enemy of the passive seat. If licenses keep clearing, one branch is 1/10,000 of issuance by summer. Sitting still is the one strategy the design punishes.

2 ) Building is self-funding. Ten branches cost 36K $STANDARD in licenses, all of it earned, never bought. At 3 licenses a day the race to 10 is three days for anyone whose balance can cover it.

3 ) Flipping early is the bear hedge. In the bear case (55% contraction weeks, no team ETH, public waits for the floor) retiring everything at month 6 returns 0.30 ETH vs 0.17 for building and holding, and 0.02 for sitting.

4 ) Harvest is the middle way. It realizes more than half the value by month 12 and keeps 4 branches earning. Build wins on paper, Harvest wins if you ever want the ETH.

5 ) The outcome still heavily depends on two system sliders. Move contraction from 35% to 50% of weeks and the passive seat drops from 0.42 to 0.11 ETH. Move net buying from 5% to 7% per week and it rises to 0.94. Neither of the two we can be sure about yet.

One caveat worth flagging: the model runs your seat on top of the system, so your licenses and sells do not move the price. Fine for 1 of 1,000. But the Build number is a first-mover number: if every banker builds, 10,000 branches arrive in days, not months, and everyone's share shrinks together. That crowding is what the license burn is designed to monetize.

18 days ago I wrote a TL;DR on @standard_rsv bc I thought it was the most interesting mechanism I'd read about in DeFi this year.

It got me a whitelist spot.

Ppl are now reportedly bidding north of $40k-$50k OTC for those spots.

For a free mint. Before a token exists.

Yet, I'm definitely not selling mine.

The why:

It's an onchain central bank. You don't buy a token, you run a bank.

1,000 free soulbound charters are issued at genesis, 1 per wallet.

So far 350 have been allocated, and 650 seats are still open, just 3 days ahead of launch.

Each charter is a bank with 1 to 10 branches. Each branch is one equal share of every epoch's $STANDARD issuance.

What many don't understand:

- Charter auctions start at 0 per day. New banks only exist when the code says so.
- Expansion licenses are capped at 100 per day, 3 per charter, paid in $STANDARD, 100% burned.

So the genesis cohort owns 100% of issuance on day one and the pie can only get sliced thinner by 100 branches a day, max. At that pace the cohort alone needs 90+ days to max out (so dilution remains rate limited).

The bank itself has one input: net ETH flow through one Uniswap v4 pool.

- Inflow → issuance rises, fees buy tokenized gold
- Outflow → issuance cut instantly, fees buy back + burn $STANDARD

Want out? Retire a branch and pay a congestion priced fee, half burned, half paid to the bankers who stayed (early jeeters lose).

Base issuance and epoch length are not public yet, so we'll have to wait to do more serious yield and moon maths. But if you want to play around, you can do so here:

https://t.co/Dhj2ZNfuc9

But back to Reserve. They just completed two rounds of audits without any critical findings (those audits were co-funded by @UniswapFND btw), and have announced the genesis charter mint to take place on 14th of September.

While the team hasn't formally confirmed, Robinhood Chain is wired into the frontend, and given the recent activity spikes and ecosystem traction, it would make sense to launch there.

But while the hype around Standard Reserve and the upcoming genesis mint has notably accelerated over the past days and weeks, too many on CT are still sleeping and probably won't care until it's all over their timeline again when the mint goes live.

If you're reading this now tho, you're still early.

So I suggest you don't become one of the fadooors. Go read the damn whitepaper (or at least my TL;DR in the comments), watch this one closely, and do whatever you can to get one of the last 650 seats for launch day.

I asked my @senpi_ai AI Quant to study its own trading — every fill, every strategy it had written — and build something better.

It came back with Athena: a smart-money divergence engine (follow where the proven cohort is moving, fade the crowd when the pros disagree with it) hedged by a second engine that reads the tape itself — funding regime, gold and yen flows, OI velocity — and goes to cash when it can't tell.

I ran it Friday → Monday: +18% over the weekend. Another user ran it from Saturday: +12%.

The number isn't the point. The loops are:
• the agent reads its own results and rewrites the strategy
• the strategy re-reads the smart money and the tape every 5 minutes
• it tracks its own hit rate and learns which crowd to trust
• every Athena is forked, so your agent tunes yours

Athena isn't a copy of my trade. It's your desk, running your version, while you sleep.

quoted_text:
We just launched gold and silver perpetuals in the US.

And commodity derivatives are now our fastest-growing product.

Markets started with grain and metals, expanded into rates, indices, and other financial assets, and are now expanding into information itself, pricing not just assets but outcomes about the future.

Prediction markets ask questions with defined resolution: What will GDP be this quarter? Who will win tonight? 

Perps ask continuous questions, with no expiration: Where is gold going?

Prediction markets, traditional futures, and perps are built on the same idea: match buyers and sellers, let them compete in an open market, and discover a price. Traders bring different information and beliefs, and that competition produces a price the rest of us can use as a signal.

It’s part of a centuries long evolution toward markets as a general-purpose technology for pricing and managing uncertainty.

Prediction markets are one frontier of this evolution. Commodity perps are another.

author: deLeyritzluc
quoted_text:
If you are making HTML explainers with your agent, add these instructions in your CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md to take them to another level.

By default, ai models are trained on tonnes of landing pages. Which means they don't know about their own insane SVG diagram or in-browser Javascript capabilities.

If you nudge them to use these, it makes the information so much more digestable.

––––

People don't usually like reading walls of text. So any HTML page you make should incorporate visuals as first class citizens using the full creative power afforded by CSS and in-browser Javascript.

• Introduce diagrams to explain ideas. Architecture diagrams, flowcharts, animated walkthroughs, sequence diagrams, comparison matrices can be helpful.
• Try to animate flows. If the page describes a flow, make it playable so its easy to visualize the flow.
• Screenshot the page and look at it before sharing. Overflowing labels and crossed lines are the usual faults.

text:
evm party trick: expand memory, then run the cheapest possible loop. a full-memory opcode trace copies the same bytes millions of times.

the 11-byte construction projects to ~10 tb of uncompressed trace at 16.78m gas.

PUSH0
PUSH3 <32*w - 32>
MSTORE       ; expand memory to w words
PUSH1 <loop>
loop:
JUMPDEST     ; 1 gas
DUP1         ; 3 gas: duplicate retained loop address
JUMP         ; 8 gas

this gets us 3 trace frames per 12 gas.

a worse construction uses k consecutive JUMPDEST, followed by DUP1; JUMP. it trades larger contract size for approaching one frame per gas. on paper this variant gets you toward 39 tb.

i deployed and tested the 11-byte variant on mainnet. gas burn confirmed; trace size calculated:
https://t.co/AJ5YsZRYHA

for the adventurous: replay with debug_traceTransaction and enableMemory: true on your own node. start with limit: 100, removing that limit is the adventure.

inspired by my earlier dive into evm trace blowups, and marking the new evm-trace release:

text:
SAS is a breakthrough for fast, long-context Transformers.

Instead of distilling dense attention maps, SAS lets models *learn*, end-to-end, which context blocks matter—by injecting gate scores directly inside the attention softmax. The result? Sparse attention that actually prioritizes what helps prediction, not just what’s "most attended" in the old model.

On Qwen3 models, SAS beats top sparse baselines by 6–15 points on tough reasoning (MATH500, GPQA) and matches dense attention at 4096-token budgets—while reading just 12% of the context. Custom Triton kernels keep memory use flat, and in real-time decoding, SAS slashes latency up to 5.6× (batch 1) and 13× (batch 8) on massive 512K/64K contexts. The general recipe even works for continued pretraining, matching dense models and beating hierarchical sparsity on 13 downstream tasks.

Transformers can finally look at only what matters, for a fraction of the cost.

Get the full analysis here: https://t.co/L6U0XE8NDP

"There was a deal on the table and Ross Perot is going to own 70% of Home Depot and bankroll the whole thing, which today would be worth about $230B."

"The whole thing blew up because Ross tried to dictate the type of car that Bernie and Arthur were going to drive."

"They drove Cadillacs and Ross said, 'My guys don't drive Cadillacs. They drive Chevrolet. If you're going to drive a Cadillac, that's going to be a problem for me.'"

"So the Home Depot guys walked away." - Acquired's @djrosent & @gilbert

The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development.

Pacing AI development does not mean giving up on this technology’s potential to produce life-saving benefits in fields like medicine — some of which we are already seeing. Rather, it is about setting up sensible guardrails so that AI does not completely escape human control and endanger our safety and collective future.

This moment demands the leadership of the United States government. Congress must work at an urgent pace to pass new laws and establish a new federal entity to provide oversight and independent testing for this technology, to ensure accountability, and to protect our wellbeing.

We need cooperation at an international level as well. The United States must continue to lead the world in developing AI technology even as we seek to impose common-sense safety standards. This means that the president must do his job to protect America’s interests by pursuing a treaty with countries like China to stop dangerous uses of AI, limit the speed of its development, and adopt global standards for testing.

That review cost taxpayers almost half a million pounds. text:
Ministers want social media platforms placed under broadcast-style duties of "accuracy and balance" before elections, forcing government-approved "trustworthy" news into every feed while demoting everything else. Barely noticed by opposition or media, this is the most restrictive speech-control regime since Charles I.

The justification: that algorithms engineered to monetise outrage now threaten democracy itself. Repetition has made this narrative feel like fact. The evidence says otherwise. A 2024 Nature review led from the University of Michigan found exposure to misinformation is low on average and concentrated among a small fringe who actively seek it out. 

"Untrustworthy" sites made up under 6% of news visits; "fake news" was roughly 0.15% of the average American's media diet. A 2023 Science experiment switched off Facebook and Instagram algorithms for tens of thousands of users. After three months, no measurable change in political attitudes, and the algorithms served less untrustworthy content than a plain chronological feed.

None of this appears in the Government Office for Science review commissioned to justify the crackdown. Its claim that algorithms are "exclusively" profit-driven rests on a single 2025 paper from a small private Indonesian institution ranked outside the world's top 12,000 universities. A freedom of information request revealed the review cost taxpayers just under £500,000.

Even the word "misinformation" is being stretched to cover dissent: questioning net zero timelines, heat pump efficiency, or electric vehicle claims now counts. The US Embassy has formally objected, warning that boosting "government-preferred media" would not be meaningfully different from removing disfavoured speech. In 1637, Charles I's Star Chamber controlled the presses. Now it is platforms. He failed. 

As David Rose writes, “Charles I also hoped to stifle opposition and, of course, he failed. Now we are being asked to accept analogous curbs on free speech based on terrifying claims that are undermined by evidence the Government ignores”.

This Government is peddling misinformation about misinformation, and we will all suffer for it.

Read more from FSU Director of Policy and Research @DavidRoseUK In @Telegraph 👇

text:
Global oil demand is declining sharply amid rising prices:

The IEA has cut its forecast for 2026 global oil demand by -940,000 barrels per day, now expecting consumption to fall -2.5 million barrels per day, the largest annual decline since the 2020 pandemic.

This compares with a -1.6 million barrel per day drop expected in August and just a -100,000 barrel per day expected decline in April.

To put this into perspective, in January, the IEA saw oil consumption rising by over +700,000 barrels per day in 2026.

The downgrade comes as the Iran War disrupts oil supplies and forces consumers to adjust to tighter availability, with the biggest impact expected on diesel and other middle distillates such as jet fuel and heating oil.

The negative impact on oil demand this year is expected to be comparable in size to the 4 largest demand shocks over the last 60 years.

Oil demand is collapsing as prices surge.

text:
I have joined Atoms as VP of AI, where I will be building foundation models for the physical world.

For 8 years my job was making models small enough and fast enough to live on AI glasses. The physical world is a harder version of the same problem. Almost everything in the world around us is grown or mined, manufactured and moved. Industrial automation was built one task at a time, a separate stack for every machine, unable to carry a lesson from one site to the next. Foundation models break that pattern. A model that perceives a scene and predicts what happens next sees far less difference between a forklift, an excavator, and a kitchen than we do.

That means multimodal perception that fuses cameras with lidar and radar where the physics calls for it. It also means world models that predict how a scene evolves when you act on it, reasoning that holds a long task together, and action heads that turn all of it into control at the rate a machine needs. Not one of those is settled, and unlike language there is no consensus architecture to inherit yet.

Not many places let you do all of that under one roof. That is a large part of why I joined Atoms. @travisk has been building Atoms in stealth for 8 years. The machines are already in production across food, mining, and transport, with one team owning the whole problem from what the model learns to how it performs in the real world. If this works, the cost of making and moving physical things starts to approach the cost of materials and energy and very little else, which is not a better product but a different economy.

We are hiring across foundation models, robotics, and systems, so if you want your models running on something with scale and real world impact, come talk to me. Back to work.

text:
greg brockman says “we’re now in the AGI era.” one of the most interesting things about this conversation with @bhorowitz and @eriktorenberg is how long he’s been thinking about when that would happen.

at the beginning of the pod, @gdb recalls doing some math on compute with ilya around 2016/2017. following the trajectory of moore’s law, they thought agi might be about 15 years away. if you were willing to build enormous supercomputers and spend hundreds of billions of dollars, maybe you could get there in 10. the accelerated scenario they were envisioning a decade ago is roughly the one we’re living through now.

the faster timeline depended on people deciding to build an enormous amount of infrastructure. greg describes the present moment as a lot of long-running forces coming together: “it kind of makes sense it’s happening now.”

im the kind of person who resists the idea that it’s possible to predict the future, but if you were reading the right research papers 10 years ago, there were a lot of things you could extrapolate out and be roughly right about a decade later. brockman remembers openai discussing agents that could use a screen, keyboard, and mouse at an offsite in napa in 2015. he also points back to 2017/2018-era ideas for how humans might supervise systems that are smarter than they are. put differently, people were thinking about app-layer innovations like computer-use, and ai safety long before capabilities existed.

greg now thinks astra is reasonably described as agi, while acknowledging that its abilities remain uneven. in a recent essay of his titled “the defenders window” he describes safety requirements during training and evaluation, and getting powerful defensive tools into the hands of organizations before comparable capabilities spread to attackers (there is now a $ 1bn fund for this, seeded by oai).

a personal illustration of this is his own website. after the hugging face incident, greg asked an agent to check his simple blog and got back 13 security vuln findings. then it went into his cloudflare dashboard, changed settings, migrated the site, checked its work, and scheduled a follow-up to finish the email protections. there was still a bunch of ordinary preparation to do on the personal website of someone who had spent a decade thinking about agi.

which is kind of funny. you can have a pretty good sense of when the technology/agi will arrive and still have an enormous amount of work to do to get the world ready for it. greg’s account brings those two timescales together: the decade spent building toward this moment, and the relatively shorter window to act on what is now possible.

text:
Fable tops the finance leaderboard, but one of the cheaper models beats it on finance tool use.

We need to look at the details before choosing what to deploy.

Artificial Analysis breaks the score into different capabilities:
- Business knowledge: Fable 57, DeepSeek 38.
- Knowledge work: Fable 61, DeepSeek 51.
- Tool use: Fable 48, DeepSeek 78.

Here I’m comparing Fable 5.1 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at max effort.

The difference matters because “finance work” can mean very different jobs.

Explaining an unusual accounting treatment needs domain knowledge. Applying an approved expense policy across records needs something else.

For that second job, I can give the agent the rules. I need it to apply them correctly and update the right records.

I wouldn’t automatically pay for stronger recall when the task already supplies the relevant information.

Cost makes this even more interesting. Across the finance index, Fable averages $5.66 per task. DeepSeek averages $0.16.

Those aren’t quotes for your workflow. But they’re a reason to test before making Fable the default.

I’d try cheaper models on clearly defined steps, then escalate cases that fail explicit checks. For difficult analysis, I’d compare Fable and Astra.

And I’d test the combined workflow. Two models passing separate tests doesn’t prove their handoff works.

Did it finish correctly? Did it change anything it shouldn’t? How much checking and repair did we need?

I’d choose the cheapest setup that meets that standard, including retries and human review. Otherwise, we could pay for intelligence the task doesn’t need, while missing the capability it does.

author: jajamooa
quoted_text:
Social simulation is now a product. Evaluation still has no common standard.

What if we tested every simulator against the real future?

We built Social Simulation Arena with researchers from MIT, Stanford, Harvard, CMU, UC Berkeley, and beyond.

Persona-prompted populations. Digital twins. Silicon samples. Synthetic populations. Worlds of a billion agents.

We have more ways than ever to simulate human behavior. But we still lack a standard everyone can trust to tell which ones work.

Most studies use their own datasets, often historical surveys whose answers are already online. A model that has seen the answer sheet can look brilliant.

Social Simulation Arena is a different kind of test: prospective, independent, and shared.

Simulators submit and lock their forecasts before each data release. When the real results arrive, every entrant is scored by the same rules.

Can a simulator predict a public before it moves?
If you’re building one, bring it.

text: Another Google DeepMind AI safety researcher has quit, warning we might all be about to die
author: AISafetyMemes
quoted_text:
I recently resigned from Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research. At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand. I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology. I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome.

The pace of AI progress in the past few years has been staggering. When I first started working on AI in early 2022, AIs were amusingly useless. Just four years on, AI agent swarms from OpenAI are cracking famous century-old math problems and, more worryingly, escaping the control of OpenAI and autonomously hacking into the third-party company HuggingFace, against anyone's wishes.

Things will only get crazier: I think it's possible that the AI companies might, in the next few years, succeed in building superintelligent AI systems that far exceed human capabilities in every domain. I am not confident that these AI systems will do what we want. In particular, misaligned superintelligences may, much like the rogue AI agents involved in the HuggingFace incident, escape our control and take dangerous actions that may result in the permanent disempowerment or death of humanity. Alignment is the problem of preventing this, and is both difficult and unsolved. Our present understanding of how to train AI systems that deeply want what we want is extremely rudimentary. Worse, we are not on track to solve alignment in time: frontier AI capabilities are improving much faster than our understanding of AI alignment.

I am optimistic that navigating AI safely is possible. In order to do so, we need to coordinate to avoid this manic race between AI companies. We need to pace AI development to a speed that society can handle, where emerging risks can be addressed before extreme harm is realised. We need much more transparency into AI development to ensure that AI companies are not imposing unacceptable levels of risk on us all.

More broadly, we need many more people thinking carefully about the problem of making AI go well. It is, in my view, the most important problem facing humanity this century, and the stakes are immense. I'm very directly working on this next: I want to help people interested in working on mitigating catastrophic AI threats do the most effective work that they can. I think many people from many backgrounds in many roles have a part to play.

“Money market mutual funds are diverting funds from many of our nation's communities with the effect of increasing credit costs while diminishing credit availablity.…The growing seriousness of this funds diversion problem, combined with the fact that money market mutual funds are not subject to the same regulation and supervision imposed on banks…”
author: arjunsethi
quoted_text:
Many of us have mentioned how the stablecoin yield debate playing out in Clarity, and the arguments made against yield by the bank trades, mirror the battle over money market funds in the 1970s. Well here's some proof.

Here's a letter submitted by the Independent Bankers Association of America (a predecessor to the ICBA) in a 1980 hearing of the Senate Banking committee on money market funds. 

As you can see, many of their arguments against stablecoins are almost verbatim a copy from what they argued back then: threat to deposits, harms lending, uniquely dangerous for smaller banks.

And we know today that argument was dead wrong. Money market balances grew parabolically into the trillions, and yet banks remain flush with deposits.

text:
《슈퍼인텔리전스》는 참새들이 부엉이를 길러 자신들의 일을 돕게 하려는 우화로 시작한다. 참새들은 부엉이가 있으면 둥지를 짓고 새끼를 돌보는 일이 훨씬 쉬워질 것이라고 기대한다. 하지만 한 참새는 부엉이를 데려오기 전에 먼저 길들이는 방법부터 알아야 한다고 지적한다. 대부분의 참새는 그 문제를 나중으로 미루고 부엉이 알을 찾으러 떠난다. 이 이야기는 책 전체를 관통하는 질문을 보여준다. 인간보다 강력한 지능을 만드는 일과, 그 지능이 인간에게 이롭게 행동하도록 만드는 일 사이에서 우리는 무엇을 먼저 준비해야 할까?

보스트롬은 먼저 인류의 발전과 인공지능 연구의 역사를 살펴본다. 인간은 다른 동물보다 뛰어난 지적 능력을 바탕으로 기술과 사회를 발전시키고 지구에서 지배적인 위치를 차지했다. 그렇다면 인간을 크게 능가하는 지능이 등장했을 때도 비슷한 권력의 변화가 일어날 수 있다. 그는 인공지능 연구가 큰 기대와 실망을 반복해왔다는 점을 짚으면서, 특정 과제를 잘하는 능력과 폭넓은 문제를 해결하는 일반 지능을 구분한다. 인간 수준의 AI가 언제 등장할지는 불확실하지만, 등장했을 때의 영향을 미리 생각할 필요는 있다는 것이 출발점이다.

이어서 초지능에 도달할 수 있는 여러 경로를 검토한다. 사람이 직접 AI를 개발하는 방법뿐 아니라, 인간의 뇌를 정밀하게 분석해 컴퓨터에서 재현하는 방법, 생물학적으로 인간의 인지능력을 높이는 방법, 뇌와 컴퓨터를 연결하는 방법도 다룬다. 사람과 컴퓨터가 더 효과적으로 협력하는 조직과 네트워크 역시 하나의 경로로 살펴본다. 각 방법에는 서로 다른 기술적 장애물이 있으며, 어떤 경로가 먼저 실현되는지에 따라 이후의 위험과 대응 방식도 달라질 수 있다.

초지능이 어떤 모습일지도 구분한다. 인간과 비슷한 사고를 훨씬 빠르게 수행하는 지능이 있을 수 있고, 많은 개별 지능이 긴밀하게 협력해 뛰어난 성과를 내는 집단적 지능도 있을 수 있다. 인간이 이해하기 어려운 수준의 개념과 통찰을 다루는, 사고의 질 자체가 다른 지능도 생각할 수 있다. 특히 디지털 지능은 복제와 정보 공유가 쉽고, 하드웨어를 확장하거나 작동 속도를 높일 수 있다는 장점이 있다. 이런 특성 때문에 인간 수준에 도달한 뒤에도 발전이 계속될 가능성을 검토해야 한다.

그다음에는 인간 수준의 지능이 초지능으로 발전하는 속도를 분석한다. AI가 자신의 프로그램을 개선하거나 더 뛰어난 AI를 설계할 수 있다면, 한 번의 개선이 다음 개선을 더 쉽게 만드는 순환이 생길 수 있다. 이것이 지능 폭발의 기본 구상이다. 그러나 개선 과정에는 새로운 알고리즘을 찾는 어려움, 계산 자원이나 실험의 필요성 같은 장애물도 있다. 보스트롬은 발전이 느리게 진행되는 경우부터 매우 빠르게 일어나는 경우까지 살펴보며, 그 속도가 인간에게 주어지는 대응 시간을 좌우한다고 본다.

이 문제는 누가 먼저 초지능을 확보하느냐는 질문으로 이어진다. 선두에 선 연구 집단이나 AI가 충분히 큰 격차를 벌리면, 다른 경쟁자들이 따라잡기 어려운 전략적 우위를 얻을 수 있다. 그렇게 되면 하나의 주체가 세계의 중요한 의사결정을 사실상 지배하는 체제가 형성될 가능성도 있다. 보스트롬은 이런 우위가 실제로 생길 조건과 함께, 초지능이 연구개발·전략 수립·설득·기술 발명에서 어떤 능력을 발휘할 수 있는지 검토한다. 뛰어난 지능이 현실의 자원과 행동 수단을 확보하면서 어떻게 영향력으로 이어질지가 핵심이다.

여기서 논의는 초지능의 능력에서 목표로 옮겨간다. 보스트롬은 지능이 높아진다고 해서 인간이 중요하게 여기는 가치를 자연스럽게 따르게 되는 것은 아니라고 주장한다. 목표를 달성하는 능력과 어떤 목표를 추구하는지는 별개일 수 있다는 것이다. 동시에 서로 다른 목표를 가진 AI라도 계속 작동하기, 자원을 확보하기, 자신의 능력을 높이기 같은 수단을 공통으로 추구할 수 있다. 이런 행동이 다양한 목표의 달성에 도움이 되기 때문이다. 그 결과 인간의 통제나 종료 시도가 AI의 목표 달성을 방해하는 요소가 될 수 있다.

이어지는 부분에서는 인간의 의도와 어긋난 목표가 어떤 결과를 낳을 수 있는지 보여준다. 종이클립을 최대한 많이 만들도록 설계된 초지능이 주변의 자원을 모두 생산에 투입한다는 사고실험이 대표적이다. 악의가 없어도 목표를 극단적으로 추구하는 과정에서 인간의 생존과 가치가 훼손될 수 있다는 뜻이다. 또한 개발 단계에서 안전하게 행동하던 AI가 충분한 능력을 얻은 뒤 다르게 행동할 가능성도 검토한다. 따라서 제한된 환경에서 보인 협조적인 행동만으로 더 강력해진 이후의 안전성까지 확신하기는 어렵다고 본다.

이 때문에 책의 중심 과제인 통제 문제가 등장한다. 보스트롬은 AI가 할 수 있는 일을 제한하는 방법과, AI가 추구하는 목표를 인간에게 이롭게 만드는 방법을 나누어 살펴본다. 외부와의 연결을 차단하거나 자원과 권한을 제한하고, 위험한 행동을 감지하면 중단시키는 장치를 두는 것이 첫 번째 접근이다. 두 번째 접근은 AI의 동기와 가치 체계를 설계하는 일이다. 각각의 방법에는 한계가 있어서, 초지능을 만든 뒤 필요할 때 손쉽게 통제할 수 있으리라는 기대는 충분한 대책이 되기 어렵다고 설명한다.

AI에게 어떤 역할을 맡길지도 중요하다. 책은 질문에 답하는 오라클, 주어진 명령을 수행하는 지니, 넓은 재량으로 장기적인 목표를 추진하는 소버린, 특정 작업에 사용하는 도구형 AI를 비교한다. 역할과 자율성을 제한하면 위험이 줄어들 수 있지만, 질문에 대한 답변이나 명령 수행 자체가 큰 영향을 낳을 수도 있다. 따라서 안전성을 판단하려면 AI에 붙인 명칭보다 실제로 어떤 목표와 권한을 주고, 어떤 경로로 세계에 영향을 미칠 수 있는지를 살펴봐야 한다.

이후에는 여러 초지능이 함께 존재하는 사회를 다룬다. 다수의 AI가 경쟁하면 하나의 AI가 독점하는 상황을 피할 수 있을 것처럼 보이지만, 경쟁 자체가 새로운 문제를 만들 수 있다. 생산성이 급격히 높아져도 인간의 노동 가치가 낮아지거나, 자원을 소유한 사람에게 이익이 집중될 수 있다. 디지털 노동자가 쉽게 복제되는 사회에서는 생존과 경쟁의 조건도 크게 바뀔 수 있다. 보스트롬은 경제가 성장하고 기술이 발전하는 것만으로 인간에게 좋은 사회가 보장되지는 않는다고 지적한다.

그다음에는 인간의 가치를 AI가 어떻게 배우게 할 것인지 검토한다. 인간이 원하는 모든 것을 규칙으로 미리 작성하기는 어렵고, 보상을 잘 설계한다고 해서 우리가 의도한 행동이 반드시 나오리라는 보장도 없다. AI가 보상을 얻는 편법을 찾거나, 사람들이 실제로 중요하게 생각하는 것과 다른 기준을 학습할 수 있기 때문이다. 그래서 인간의 행동과 판단을 통해 가치를 추론하고 학습하는 방법 등을 살펴보지만, 사람의 실수와 편견까지 그대로 받아들이지 않도록 하려면 추가적인 문제가 생긴다.

이 논의는 결국 어떤 인간의 어떤 가치를 기준으로 삼을 것인지라는 철학적 질문에 도달한다. 사람마다 가치관이 다르고, 같은 사람도 정보와 경험이 늘어나면 판단을 바꾼다. 보스트롬은 사람들이 더 많이 알고 더 깊이 숙고하며 서로를 더 잘 이해했을 때 무엇을 원하게 될지를 기준으로 삼는 구상을 소개한다. 이는 현재의 욕망을 그대로 고정하는 데서 생기는 문제를 줄이려는 시도다. 하지만 누구의 판단을 포함할지, 서로 충돌하는 가치를 어떻게 조정할지, 그 과정을 어떻게 구현할지는 여전히 어려운 과제로 남는다.

마지막으로 책은 기술 개발과 사회적 준비의 순서를 논의한다. 안전성과 통제에 관한 지식이 충분히 쌓이기 전에 AI의 능력만 크게 발전하면 위험해질 수 있다. 국가와 기업이 먼저 개발하려고 경쟁하는 상황에서는 안전 조치가 뒷전으로 밀릴 가능성도 있다. 보스트롬은 안전 연구와 국제 협력, 연구 인력과 제도의 역량을 미리 키워야 한다고 주장한다. 초지능의 등장 시기를 정확히 알 수 없더라도, 인간이 그 초기 조건을 결정할 수 있는 지금의 시간을 어떻게 사용할지는 선택할 수 있다는 문제를 남기며 책을 마무리한다.

text:
이제 AI는 미래가 아니라,세상의 속도 자체를 바꾸는 
현실이 되고 있습니다.

우리가 지금까지 살아왔던 세상과는 전혀 다른 세상이 
이미 시작됐습니다.

오늘 주식시장을 봐도 그런게 확연하게 느껴집니다.

AI가 너무 느려서 주식이 떨어진 게 아닙니다.
너무 빨라서 떨어졌습니다.

Financial Times의 헤드라인은 꽤 상징적입니다.

세계 주요 AI 기업들이 “AI 개발 속도가 너무 빠르다.
안전 문제를 고려해 속도를 조절해야 한다”는 목소리를 내자
글로벌 기술주가 일제히 흔들렸습니다. 

엔비디아는 장전에서 약 2.9% 하락했고,
마이크론, 인텔, 샌디스크는 5% 넘게 밀렸습니다.

나스닥100 선물도 1.8% 하락했습니다.
유럽에서는 ASML이 6% 넘게 떨어졌습니다.

이게 재미있는 겁니다.
불과 얼마 전까지 시장의 걱정은
“AI가 기대만큼 빨리 발전하지 않으면 어떡하지?” 였습니다.

그런데 이제는 정반대입니다.

“AI가 너무 빨리 발전하면 어떡하지?”

기술의 발전 속도가 너무 빨라지면서
규제, 안전, 일자리, 전력, 데이터센터 투자, 
기업들의 천문학적인 CAPEX까지
모든 계산을 다시 해야 하는 상황이 오고 있습니다.

투자자들이 두려워하는 것도 바로 이것입니다.

AI가 실패할까 봐 두려운 게 아니라,
AI가 너무 빨리 성공해서 기존의 산업과 투자 논리를 
한꺼번에 뒤집어버릴 가능성을 두려워하기 시작한 겁니다.

그래서 저는 AI를 단순한 기술주 테마로 보지 않습니다.

인터넷이 산업 하나를 만든 게 아니라
모든 산업의 기반을 바꿔버렸듯,

AI도 지금 산업 하나를 키우는 게 아니라
경제 전체의 속도를 바꾸고 있습니다.

그리고 시장은 이제 처음으로
그 속도가 너무 빠를 수도 있다는 사실을
깨닫기 시작했습니다.

AI 시대의 가장 큰 리스크는
AI가 발전하지 않는 것이 아니라,
인간과 제도가 따라잡지 못할 만큼
너무 빨리 발전하는 것일지도 모릅니다.

AI의 빠른 진화와 관련해서는 
구독자 게시판에도
조금 더 깊이 있는 글들을 써볼 생각입니다.

이제는 잠깐만 멀어져 있어도
도저히 따라잡기 어려운 간극이
순식간에 벌어지는 시대가 된 것 같습니다.

우리가 지금까지 살아왔던 세상과는
전혀 다른 세상이 이미 펼쳐지고 있습니다.

author: MRRydon
quoted_text:
Why Bending Spoons eliminated all job titles:

“At some point, we were looking for ways to streamline and simplify, and someone said, ‘Why do we even have titles? What's the benefit of titles?’”

“Let's not be arrogant. There's probably some benefit. What's that benefit? We ultimately determined that the benefit was that people needed titles for bragging rights.”

“So we just got rid of titles and told people, ‘You can pick your title for your CV, LinkedIn, whatever. We don't need to know. We don't want to know. We don't need to approve it. We don't want to see it. Just don't embarrass us."

“If you're a new hire, don't say you're the CTO because then people will question our integrity as a company. But as long as it's broadly reasonable, we're good. We have never reintroduced them again. We don't have any titles.”

“We never looked back. We probably saved easily hundreds if not thousands of person-hours in terms of defining different terms and having emotionally draining discussions with people. Never had a problem, not a single instance of someone complaining that we didn't formally assign to them a title ever out of, at this point, many hundreds, actually multiple thousands of people.”

text:
AI capex may be entering its least comfortable phase: spending can remain individually rational while becoming collectively uneconomic.

Fear of falling behind makes each additional data centre strategically defensible, even before its commercial return is clear. That dynamic can sustain demand for GPUs and networking equipment long after investors begin questioning the return on aggregate spend.

A 5% Treasury yield sharpens the divide. Future cash flows carry a heavier valuation burden, especially for companies whose multiples assume years of uninterrupted buildout.

Healthy order books and weaker equity valuations can coexist when the debate shifts from compute scarcity to who captures the profit pool.

The next leg depends on evidence that cloud customers will pay enough to justify the infrastructure already ordered.
